summary: Liquid and cigarette/pipe objects distinguish I.1 drinking from I.2 smoking across texts. Tobacco smoking is already lexicalized; agentive šatoyo adds habitual smoker predicates in Part act. 2.

The inherited Detransitive Infinitiv štoyo has generic active event/provision readings. Retain its filing convention and inherited sense key 1; do not invent a separately numbered Detransitive sense or interpret the noun as a patient-subject form.
III drinkers occur as zero-marked animal/human NPs and l-suffixes; liquids are often unexpressed. Animal watering remains III.1, garden irrigation III.3, and textile frame preparation III.2.

Preterit can summarize repeated watering over a week (JL15.6/12). Infectum-wa marks habitual drinking and service as well as irrealis; ko-Preterit and the unusual ko Imperativ are already represented.

Prym–Socin citations in the entry use page/line (prs27/13,147/29,171/35,213/36,214/11), whereas supplied PrS references use text/verse. Similar wording does not warrant replacing one with the other. No fix-citation asserted on that basis.
Round 2 is based on the supplied Jan Turoyo; accompanying English is project machine translation [MT]. Round 1 was read first and its proposals are not duplicated.

Round 1 already brings literal Preterit above five, Infectum to five, Infectum-wa to five and Imperativ to five, and smoking Preterit/Infectum to five. Routine Jan suggestions for these cells are not added.

Infinitiv štoyo has generic provisioning/consumption and smoking readings. The inherited Detransitive heading is a filing convention: nominal possession -ayḏe/-ayḏa and the b- event complement do not indicate an affected subject.

Causative maštanwolanyo (Jan 1.36/1526) resumes drinkers and liquid; maštəleli qaḥwe/čay has an explicit liquid and recipient suffix (Jan 1.39/1711; 1.42/1857). Inanimate stencil plus ink extends the same uptake frame.

Bare Infectum with lo is a negative instruction (Jan 3.39/1121,1123), not Imperativ. Preterit štelox in iḏa (Jan 2.10/2307) is hypothetical despite its morphology. Narrative kšutena and kšuteno retain Infectum classification.

III Preterit 2 and Preterit-wa corrections were already made in round 1; do not duplicate them. The drinking-well proverb (Jan 2.12/2873) uses ordinary literal syntax inside a moral comparison, not a new lexical idiom.
Confirm šatye at 57/92: is it a resultative Part. Pass. with drinkers as subject, a distinct participial pattern, or a Part act. variant? It is withheld from box additions.
Confirm the segmentation of štannanne (65/51), masculine kšoto (PrS26/18), and the relationship of maštyo/štayo provision nouns to Infinitiv štoyo.
Verify 24/295 versus inherited 24/296 and the noted unlocated 11/116 example against the edition before changing citations.
PrS60/67's supplied translation omits the maštewo relative clause; obtain the matching edition text before quoting that occurrence.
Does the figurative city-consuming pair denote expenditure, possession, or a broader boast in each text? Preserve its documented range without forcing one historical interpretation.
Does maštəlalla (Jan 2.4/848) contain a plural causer plus stencil recipient suffix, or another segmentation? Verify against šty III maštele; do not silently regularize it.
Confirm the relation of šatyo (Jan 2.10/2316), evaluative šatoyo (Jan 2.10/2308), and activity šatoye (Jan 2.35/5664). Round 1 already withheld šatye as a paradigm example.
Check the physical referent and šeno at Jan 2.29/4747; the supplied English simultaneously says dry and wet and cannot settle the matter.
At Jan 1.49/2194, Štay is morphologically Imperativ despite the question mark. Keep punctuation; do not use the English perfect question to reclassify it.
At Jan 2.10/2310, is šutele ordinary drinking with beneficiary -le or an unprefixed local causative? Withhold that example pending confirmation.
Check quotation boundaries and the speaker shift in Jan 3.39/1123; do not treat the doctors as the first-person drinker.
